paper_title: ProTEUS: A mutation-resolved world model for closed-loop protein evolution

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Protein engineering requires navigating rugged fitness landscapes, where small sequence changes can produce large functional differences, but experimental screening can only sample a small fraction of sequence space. Thus, a central challenge is to efficiently traverse the large combinatorial space of mutations in silico. We introduce ProTEUS, a mutation-resolved world model for closed-loop protein evolution. Pretrained on deep mutational scanning assays, ProTEUS learns a joint representation of sequence, evolutionary, and structural information using MutationFormer, a mutation-biased attention architecture. Variants are represented as states in this joint latent space, and mutations define actions whose functional consequences are predicted. To support exploration of many mutants, we developed a fast, physics-constrained all-atom predictor that utilizes explicit geometric constraint enforcement to achieve >10 fold increase in speed than AlphaFold3 with guaranteed physical validity. Lastly, ProTEUS refines its prediction and understanding of protein activity through closed loop experimental feedback to guide evolution toward a desired phenotype. ProTEUS surpasses established models in both zero-shot and supervised fine-tuning mutation prediction tasks. We experimentally demonstrate its utility in two closed-loop multi-objective engineering campaigns on aldehyde dehydrogenase and levansucrase, yielding variants with >10 fold higher activity than wild type. ProTEUS provides a world-model framework that connects virtual evaluation of mutational outcomes with experimental learning for efficient protein evolution.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Protein engineering expands the capabilities of biotechnology and medicine by improving desired activity beyond what is offered in nature including catalytic activity, binding affinity, stability and expression (13). Directed evolution has played central role in this pursuit, which achieves these goals through repeated mutation and selection, but experimental screening, including continuous directed evolution techniques, can only sample small fraction of the full sequence space (4, 5). Although deep mutational scanning for all single mutants of protein is possible, epistasis still complicates the route to find the best sequence which may process multiple mutations from wild-type (WT) (68). central challenge is thus to build computational model to evaluate large number of mutations in silico to guide selection of sequences for experimental testing and then use experimental feedback to improve activity predictions for successive rounds of variant selection toward desired phenotype (3, 9, 10). Various models have been deployed to score mutations in zero-shot setting to reduce the initial experimental workload in protein engineering campaign before target specific measurements are obtained. Sequence-based models, including the ESM family, learn from natural proteins and use amino acid likelihoods to estimate substitution effects (1114). MSA family-specific evolutionary Transformer, Tranception, PoET and Protriever information (1518), whereas inverse folding models like ESM-IF and ProteinMPNN assess sequence compatibility with specified protein backbone (19, 20). Multimodal models such as ESM-3, SaProt and ProSST combine sequence and structural information (2123) and local geometry, residue contacts and molecular surfaces could provide further context for enhanced prediction (2426). Lastly, retrieval-augmented models can incorporate homologous sequences and evolutionary information to help with mutational effect prediction (27, 28). Together, these approaches support virtual screening through estimates of evolutionary plausibility and structural compatibility, but so far still exhibit only moderate level of correlation with experimentally measured protein activity especially for proteins that are less represented in evolution (3, 29). incorporate The moderate performance of these zero-shot predictions can be partly attributed to the misalignment between evolutionary selection and particular activity being optimized. Natural sequence distributions reflect selection across biological constraints for particular organism, which can differ significantly from the activity targeted in an experiment (30). Favorable sequence, structural or evolutionary scores therefore do not guarantee higher protein activity (1, 3, 30). To circumvent this problem, functional measurements can be integrated to adapt the model to an engineering objective (31). In this pursuit, EVOLVEpro uses protein language model representations to guide iterative evolution from small experimental datasets (3). MULTI-evolve uses similar approach on higher order mutants (1). However, these two models still suffer from low hit rates in selecting high-activity initial set of mutations for experimental characterization and poor generalization to untested mutants, especially higher-order mutants, during active learning. In light of these challenges, we developed ProTEUS, world model for closed-loop PROTein Evolution with high mUtation reSolution (Fig. 1A-C). Inside ProTEUS, protein variants are represented as states in joint embedding space of sequence, evolutionary and structural information. We pretrained this joint latent representation on 182 deep mutational scanning (DMS) assays spanning 161 protein backgrounds with diverse protein properties including stability, organismal fitness, activity, expression and binding (29). At its core, MutationFormer aligns sequence, structural, and multiple sequence alignment (MSA) features residue by residue and integrates them through attention biased toward mutations (Fig. 1D). This design focuses the models attention on the mutations defining candidate while allowing their predicted effects to depend on the surrounding protein context. To supply physically valid structural inputs for large libraries of higher-order candidates, we developed fast, physics-constrained all-atom predictor. The predictor combines two denoising steps with differentiable GaussSeidel projection to enforce geometric and stereochemical constraints during training and inference for the joint (32). The resulting structures provide candidate-specific spatial context representation, supporting virtual evaluation of proposed mutations before laboratory testing. During pretraining, ProTEUS exhibited data-scaling behavior with respect to protein activity data (Fig. 2C), as seen in the training of large language models (LLM) and protein language models (PLM) where increase in training input data or model size leads to better performance and generalization. This reveals potentially new axis of scaling for protein engineering foundation models to capitalize on more protein activity data of various forms. ProTEUS guides successive rounds of evolution through nomination strategy linked to experimental feedback (Fig. 1C). Zero-shot scores guide the initial selection of high-fitness variants for experimental testing. Measurements from each round update activity predictions, and the nomination strategy combines these predictions with accumulated experimental evidence to select subsequent higher order candidates. Computational benchmarks show improved mutation-effect prediction in both zero-shot and supervised fine-tuning settings relative to the evaluated baselines. ProTEUS also improves higher-order fitness prediction and recovery of high-fitness variants during simulated evolution compared to EVOLVEpro and MULTI-evolve. In laboratory evolution of levansucrase and aldehyde dehydrogenase, ProTEUS can find variants with >10 fold higher activity than the starting wild-type protein within an experimental budget of 100 sequences. Together, these results establish world-model framework that links predicted mutational consequences to experimental observations, enabling experimental learning to guide protein evolution toward desired functions.

sections.title: Results
sections.content: Mutation-resolved learning improves protein fitness prediction For scoring mutational effect on protein activity, where most of the benchmarks and datasets center on single mutants (29, 33), evaluation requires distinguishing candidate states that share most of their sequence but differ substantially in function. Conventionally, pooling residue-level features into single protein representation is used but this can obscure local information relevant to prediction (13, 34, 35). The challenge thus is to focus the attention on the few substituted residues while preserving the surrounding context that determines their effects. Selective attention and gating can emphasize information relevant to prediction (3639), while controlling anomalous activations can reduce attention and feature-map artifacts (40). These principles motivate us to build mutation-resolved representation in which mutations receive explicit attention and are interpreted jointly with their sequence, evolutionary and structural context (Fig. 1D). In particular, amino acid identity, MSA and structural features were aligned residue by residue, and an explicit mutation mask marked differences from the wild-type (WT) sequence. MutationFormer integrated these features through 12-layer transformer with attention biased toward substituted positions, while retaining the surrounding protein as context. To establish this joint embedding space, we pretrained ProTEUS on 182 substitution DMS assays from ProteinGym (29) to predict measured variant fitness from multimodal inputs (Fig. 1E, tables S1-2). The pretraining data includes experimentally measured stability, organismal fitness, activity, expression and binding across human, prokaryotic, other eukaryotic and viral proteins (Fig. 2A). We screened 217 ProteinGym assays against 38 reference sequences from held-out datasets reserved for downstream evaluation to test model generalization. After excluding assays that matched these evaluation targets or met the sequence-homology exclusion criteria, we retained 182 assays for pretraining. We characterized sequence and structural level of homology to make sure there is no aberrant leakage and found no hits with 30% sequence-identity that are either above 50% query-coverage thresholds or query-normalized TM-scores 0.5 for structural threshold. (fig. S1). Within this pretraining data, ProTEUS achieved Spearman correlation of 0.933 and mean squared error (MSE) of 0.115 on the test set. To compare different model architectures ability to learn this mutational dataset, we adopted similar training procedure and found that PoET-2, the strongest evaluated baseline by rank correlation in this comparison, only achieved 0.861, showing ProTEUSs ability to use joint latent space to efficiently learn mutational effect on protein activity (41) (Fig. 2B). We next quantified how the world models predictive accuracy scaled with functional pretraining data. With the architecture and evaluation sets held fixed, increasing training data 80-fold reduced test MSE from 0.262 to 0.115, 56.3% reduction (Fig. 2C). Across the measured range, MSE followed an approximate power-law relationship with training-data size. This fit corresponded to an approximately 12.1% reduction in MSE for each doubling of training data. Spearman correlation of the held out test set increased concurrently from 0.842 to 0.933, showing that additional supervision improved both numerical fitness prediction and variant ranking. Although absolute gains diminished as the dataset expanded, both metrics continued to identify experimental activity improve at fraction. These results training largest the measurements as potential scalable source of supervision for refining the world models predictions of untested variants. Next, we used ablations to assess the contributions of mutation-biased attention and multimodal context to fitness prediction (Fig. 2D). Removing mutation bias from an otherwise matched model reduced Spearman correlation from 0.840 to 0.606; bias strength of 10 performed best among the values tested. In the input-modality comparison, sequence representations alone achieved correlation of 0.807, whereas joint sequence, MSA and structural representations achieved 0.938. Redundancy filtering and weighted sampling of MSAs produced similar performance (Fig. 2D). Together, these comparisons supported both explicit attention to substituted residues and multimodal integration of proteins evolutionary and structural context for optimal understanding of mutational effect.

S2A). therefore We then tested whether zero-shot predictions supported the selection of high-fitness variants, since most protein engineering campaigns rely on an initial set of high activity single mutants to build combinatorial libraries. In this pursuit, MULTI-evolve previously reported method by taking an ensemble of four deep learning models predictions with high accuracy (1). To benchmark ProTEUS against MULTI-evolve, we compared their zero-shot rankings across 13 held-out single-substitution DMS assays (fig. S2B) and evaluated variant selection under matched selection budgets. Among the 10 highest-ranked candidates, 75.4% selected by ProTEUS and 64.6% selected by MULTI-evolve had fitness at or above the assay mean (Fig. 2F), showing ProTEUSs superiority compared to ensemble methods. These results support the use of the pretrained world model to prioritize candidate variants on new protein backgrounds, providing starting point for experimental evolution before target-specific feedback becomes available. To assess how well the model can leverage experimental measurements on particular activity to further guide engineering, we evaluated supervised fine-tuning on the held-out DMS assays using within-assay fivefold cross-validation. On held-out variants, ProTEUS achieved mean Spearman correlation of 0.549, compared with 0.367 for ProteinNPT (34), the next-ranked method (Fig. 2G). Lastly, to evaluate whether the model can efficiently use low-N measurements to guide engineering in an active learning fashion, we simulated directed evolution on 10 single-mutant DMS datasets. ProTEUS and EVOLVEpro each selected 30 variants per round from the same candidate library over five rounds. Measurements for selected variants were revealed and used to update the model before the next round. By round 5, ProTEUS reached mean normalized best fitness of 0.741, compared with 0.555 for EVOLVEpro (Fig. 2H). Overall, these computational benchmarks support ProTEUS as state-of-the-art model for zero-shot recommendation of mutations and supervised fine-tuning on target specific activity data. Efficient physics-constrained model supports multi-mutant screening To efficiently sample large number of mutations in silico, especially for higher-order variants that differ in multiple residues, ProTEUS would need to generate high quality structures with atomic level precision and minimal computational cost per structure to supply as input (32). Current frontier structural prediction models like AlphaFold3 still suffer from poor physical validity and relatively large computational budget due to the use of diffusion modules (42), so we developed fast all-atom predictor that combined two denoising steps with explicit geometric constraint enforcement (32). The predictor retained the atom-attention encoder, MSA module and PairFormer of Boltz-1 (43), which provided conditioning features for diffusion network initialized from its released weights. The network generated provisional all-atom coordinates, and differentiable GaussSeidel projection corrected geometric and stereochemical violations (Fig. 3A-B). At inference, projection followed the second denoising update. The learned predictor thus recovered molecular conformation, while the projection enforced local constraints on the resulting coordinates. The projection balanced correction of constraint violations against displacement from the predicted structure. Seven constraint families covered nonbonded tetrahedral chirality, E/Z double-bond stereochemistry, carbon inter-chain separation, double-bond planarity, ligand internal distances, symmetric-chain overlap and inter-chain covalent bonds (Fig. 3B; table S3). The solver exploited constraint locality by updating affected coordinates in place and using each correction in subsequent updates. Twenty GaussSeidel sweeps resolved coupled constraints without assembling large global system (32). Constraints without shared atoms were processed in parallel on the GPU to reduce the cost of geometric correction. We included projection during training so that the predictor learned to generate coordinates compatible with the subsequent correction. The Boltz-1-initialized network was fine-tuned on approximately 180,000 Protein Data Bank structures, with the denoising loss evaluated on projected coordinates. Implicit differentiation propagated gradients through the projection without storing the full sequence of solver iterations. In the reported CASP15 ablation (32), fine-tuning through projection increased complex LDDT from 0.5889 to 0.6321 relative to inference-only projection. Both settings passed all seven validity checks. The fine-tuned two-step predictor approached the complex LDDT of 0.6406 obtained with the 200-step Boltz-1 reference. Training through projection therefore helped retain structural accuracy under reduced denoising budget. We evaluated structural accuracy and geometric validity across CASP15, Test, PoseBusters, AF3-AB, dsDNA and RNAprotein benchmarks. Global accuracy, measured by complex LDDT (44) and TM-score (45), was broadly comparable to the evaluated baselines, and all projected structures passed the seven validity checks (Fig. 3C), when baseline predictions did not consistently satisfy these checks. The complete inference procedure, including denoising and projection, achieved median 9.4-fold speedup over 200-step Boltz-1 on CASP15 (32) (Fig. 3D). Across five atom-count bins, AlphaFold 3 mean runtimes were 7.8110.81 times higher than those of our predictor. In the representative proteinligand complex PDB 7WCF, AlphaFold 3 predicted ligandside-chain separation of 1.41 Å, whereas our predictor yielded 4.44 Å, reflecting more accurate resolution of local geometry that is critical for variety of downstream tasks including molecular dynamics and protein engineering (Fig. 3E). Higher-order mutation activity prediction Virtual exploration of higher-order variants requires predicting functional outcomes beyond the mutation order covered by existing measurements. We therefore tested whether ProTEUS could generalize from measured lower-order variants to higher-order combinations. In K-vs-rest benchmark across 15 multi-mutant DMS datasets, models were trained on variants carrying up to substitutions and tested on variants carrying more than (46). For this task, we compared ProTEUS directly with MULTI-evolve for higher-order fitness prediction (Fig. 3F). Across 40 datasets-K comparisons, ProTEUS achieved mean Spearman correlation of 0.448, compared with 0.295 for MULTI-evolve. Among these comparisons, ProTEUS achieved higher correlation in 80%, reflecting more information-rich joint embedding space ProTEUS uses. We then evaluated whether predictions updated with new measurements could guide successive rounds of higher-order variant selection. We compared ProTEUS with EVOLVEpro and MULTI-evolve in simulations of progressive directed evolution on 17 DMS datasets. We also included an additive model fitted to accumulated measurements, providing baseline for variant selection based on individual substitution effects without interaction terms (47). Each method selected 30 variants per round from the same candidate library over five model-guided rounds following an initial batch. Measurements for selected variants were revealed and used to update the model before the next round. ProTEUS achieved the highest mean normalized best fitness in each round (Fig. 3G), extending its predictive performance to iterative exploration of mutation combinations. Based on these results, we finalized ProTEUSs closed-loop evolution strategy by prompting ProTEUS to zero-shot rank an initial single-mutant batch. Subsequent nominations combined zero-shot scores, updated fitness predictions and fitness ranks derived from all available experimental measurements (fig. S4; table S4). The highest-ranked eligible, untested variants were selected, with the maximum allowed mutation order retained or increased by one. Measurements from each batch updated the model and the experimental evidence available for subsequent nominations. Agentic Closed-loop evolution of levansucrase with ProTEUS To smoothly integrate ProTEUS with wet-lab and the growing capabilities of LLMs, we built an agentic workflow to automate the end to end closed-loop protein evolution (Fig. 4A). An agent coordinates sequence candidates generation, fitness prediction, mutation nomination, and incorporates experimental feedback to update the model for subsequent rounds. Beyond workflow automation, the agent supports scientific assessment of the mutations proposed by ProTEUS. ProTEUS prioritizes the top-k candidate mutation sites, and the agent combines ProTEUS scores with LLM-based analysis of the physicochemical implications of the proposed substitutions to generate rationale and confidence assessment for each nominated variant. These assessments accompany the ranked candidates in human-in-the-loop review step, helping scientists evaluate the proposed substitutions and make informed choices about mutation sites for experimental testing. As modern LLMs get increasingly knowledgeable about diverse proteins, these assessments could also be incorporated as part of scoring function in the future (48). To evaluate ProTEUS-guided evolution, we followed the predefined variant-nomination strategy from our computational benchmarks. For the two closed loop engineering campaigns shown here, agent-generated rationales and confidence assessments served as interpretive annotations, without human adjustment of candidate rankings or batch selection based on these assessments. We first deployed agentic ProTEUS to engineer levansucrase (SacB) from Bacillus subtilis. Levansucrase transfers fructosyl groups from sucrose to synthesize levan, releasing glucose (49). Levan's use as viscosifier, stabilizer and gelling agent in variety of food applications motivates efforts to improve its enzymatic activity and stability (50). To generate high throughput levansucrase activity and expression data, we cloned mutations suggested by ProTEUS into his tagged vector for expression in E. coli and then measured glucose production from sucrose breakdown to infer catalytic activity of the enzyme (Fig. 4A). In addition, we can measure the expression of the enzyme directly by an anti-His tag ELISA. Using this setup, we performed multi-objective engineering by considering the product of expression and catalytic activity as the reward function since mutations that only improve activity but compromise expressions and stability are not useful in downstream applications. ProTEUS started with an initial zero-shot recommendation of 30 single mutants, and laboratory testing revealed that Q34N mutant within this batch had 4.5-fold higher activity than the WT protein, reaffirming the ability to zero-shot identify high fitness candidates as seen in previous computational benchmarks (Fig. 4B-C). Subsequently, ProTEUS used this data to suggest higher-order mutants in round wise fashion (Fig. 4B). The next round identified Q34N:G240W and Q34N:S359F with activities of 8.94-fold and 8.91-fold WT, respectively (Fig. 4C). Both double-mutant parents were carried forward by ProTEUS, allowing proper exploration of two backgrounds with similar measured activities. In the third experimental batch, ProTEUS suggested 18 triple mutants derived from Q34N:G240W and 12 derived from Q34N:S359F (table S5). In the third round, G23A:Q34N:G240W reached 14.03-fold WT activity, 1.57 times that of its parent, while Q34N:M328L:S359F reached 12.38-fold WT activity (Fig. 4C, fig. S5A; table S10). Q34N:G240W:Y436E also exceeded the preceding round's best variant, reaching 10.56-fold WT activity. Similar to our computational benchmarks, ProTEUS can properly identify synergistic mutations during exploration of higher-order mutations. Overall, ProTEUS was able to find variants with >10 fold higher activity than the starting WT with budget of <100 experimental tests, highlighting its ability to efficiently leverage experimental data for closed-loop evolution. To better understand the mutations explored in this closed-loop evolution, we examined how the scores used to evaluate candidates relate to measured activity within each experimental batch. Initial zero-shot scores had Spearman correlation of 0.24 with measured activity. It is worth noting that even though the initial zero-shot batch of 30 mutants properly identified high fitness variants like Q34N, the overall low global spearman correlation still highlights the divergence between model inferred protein fitness and the specific enzymatic activity and expression being optimized in this campaign. Composite scores that incorporated experimental data in the subsequent rounds were positively correlated with activity, with correlations of 0.24 in round 1 and 0.38 in round 2, reflecting the models ability to leverage experimental data to align its output to the specific engineering objective (Fig. 4D). Structural mapping placed the selected substitutions in several regions of the protein (Fig. 4E). In the WT structure, Q34 and G240 were 29.5 Å and 10.5 Å from the superposed sucrose, respectively. The alternative branch included S359, 7.6 Å from sucrose, and M328, 19.0 Å away. Similar to previously reported, these mutations do not fall in the key catalytic active site of the enzyme and thus likely contributed to the overall improvement in activity through other complementary mechanisms (3). To examine the candidate states explored during evolution, we mapped WT and the 90 assayed variants onto shared t-SNE projection containing 366,836 library representations (51). The overlaid lineage traced successive additions of Q34N, G240W and G23A in this visualization of the model latent space (Fig. 4F). We then assessed how the original 768-dimensional representation distinguished candidates within each final-round parental background. Among pairs differing at two residues, cosine distances ranged from 0.00151 to 0.03240 on Q34N:G240W and from 0.00310 to 0.03195 on Q34N:S359F (table S9). Within the Q34N:G240W background, 6 principal components were enough to capture 90% of the model representation variance, compared with 14 for the amino-acid one-hot representations used in MULTI-evolve (table S9). We next assessed the novelty of the mutations suggested by ProTEUS. In an alignment of 2,451 homologous sequences, serine was the consensus residue at position 34, occurring in 63 of 188 aligned sequences (33.5%). However, Q34S had only 0.56-fold WT activity, whereas Q34N reached 4.50-fold WT activity despite asparagine occurring in only 7 of 188 sequences (3.72%). This highlights ProTEUSs ability to deduce novel mutations that are potentially beneficial to protein activity, without overrelying on evolutionary information. In the closed-loop evolution campaigns, all three substitutions in the final lead introduced non-consensus residues. The residues introduced by G23A and G240W occurred in 6 of 184 (3.26%) and 4 of 1,258 (0.32%) aligned sequences, respectively. The originality ratios for G23A, Q34N and G240W were 0.04, 0.11 and 0.01 (Fig. 4G). Across the campaign, the 89 distinct substitutions at 65 positions had median introduced-residue frequency of 1.19%, and 22 were unobserved at their respective alignment positions. These measurements showed that the search retained beneficial substitutions that were uncommon among homologs while pursuing further improvements on experimentally supported backgrounds. Closed-loop evolution identifies improved ALDH To better understand whether ProTEUSs capability generalizes beyond one enzyme tested, we next applied ProTEUS to engineer aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH) from Cupriavidus pinatubonensis. ALDH catalyzes the oxidation of aldehydes to carboxylic acids. Human genetics have shown that mutation in the ALDH gene can lead to build up of acetaldehyde and is implicated with increased risk of cardiovascular disease and cancer (5254). To identify more potent ALDH enzyme, we established high-throughput assay to measure total ALDH activity in E. coli lysates by detecting NADH generated during acetaldehyde oxidation with coupled reaction that converted colorless probe into product absorbing at 450 nm. sections.title: Discussion
sections.content: Efficiently finding set of mutations that will push the protein toward desired phenotype is one of the holy grails of molecular engineering. In the vast space of 20L possible mutations that is not possible to experimentally characterize, any computational methods that can identify path that leads to desired activity is of great value, especially for activity not explored in nature but critical for biotechnology applications. In the age of generative protein design, many models, especially large pretrained foundation models, have been developed to rank protein variants in zero-shot fashion. However, this class of method in general suffers from the fact that many protein activities are not well represented in evolution. In contrast, active learning methods like EVOLVEpro demonstrated that pretrained protein representations can guide protein engineering (single mutant) by using relatively little experimental data points to align the model directly to experimental activity of interest (3), and MULTI-evolve has further shown that it is possible to guide engineering of higher-order variants (1). These two models highlight the utility of active learning to align model output with wet lab-measured protein activity, but still suffer from the lack of good unified representation of protein variants to efficiently leverage experimental data and guide engineering toward higher order mutations with complex epistasis (47). With an ever increasing capability of DNA synthesis, sequencing and more powerful deep learning models, we propose new way to look at this task, world model that connects the virtual evaluation of proposed mutations with experimental learning. In essence, such world model would need high quality latent space to understand and reason given mutations impact on protein phenotype and leverage experimental measurement in an efficient manner to guide models search inside this vast sequence space. To build prototype of this world model, we leveraged MutationFormer that integrates sequence, evolutionary and structural context to learn joint embedding space capable of understanding sparse mutations impact on protein activity, with physics-constrained structural predictor that significantly accelerates generation of candidate-specific structural inputs. ProTEUS achieves higher accuracy on both zero-shot ranking of protein variants and supervised fine tuning tasks where we test whether the model can efficiently learn from experimental data to extrapolate target-specific activity landscape. Our experimental validation on ALDH and levansucrase presents preliminary evidence for the utility of such model to guide protein engineering in closed-loop fashion. There are numerous ways ProTEUS could be further improved. First, the pretraining of far hosts around 2.5 million mutational ProTEUS measurements (29). In many deep learning models, especially modern day LLMs, more data during pretraining generally leads to better model performance and generalization. This scaling leveraged ProteinGym, which so law both in terms of pretraining data and model size has been the driver of breakthroughs in areas like natural language processing, computer vision, and is also seen in protein structural prediction and protein language model (5559). The data-scaling analysis showed that ProTEUS predicted held-out variant fitness more accurately as the amount of functional pretraining data increased (Fig. 2C). Protein mutation datasets typically are very noisy with strong variance even for the same protein from different sources due to the sensitive nature of different assays and measurement conditions, and thus have far fewer high quality curation compared to other domains. However, with initiatives like the ProteinGym (29) and better standardization of high throughput protein activity datasets similar to early efforts in the protein structural domains that resulted in protein data bank, we should expect an accumulation of high the coming decade, and quality mutation datasets on diverse protein activities correspondingly greater model performance and generalization for pretrained models like ProTEUS. With the rise of LLMs for text processing, it is also plausible that comprehensive mining of literatures for scattered mutation experiments will lead to collection of activity dataset for pretraining. Together, these directions represent exciting new avenues to further test the scaling behavior of protein engineering world models. in Second, we have also explored the axis of active learning size in this study (fig. S3). Similar to previous reports, larger amounts of experimental data in closed-loop evolution campaign lead to better performance. The agentic feature of ProTEUS and the rise of wet lab automation thus represent new exciting frontier where autonomous collections of wet lab experimental datapoints are guided by the model to continuously update its weight for optimal search of the protein sequence landscape (6062). These data points not only guide models current engineering campaign on specific target phenotype, but also could be used as training data in future pre-training, creating positive feedback loop. ProTEUS puts the protein engineering task into mutation-resolved world-model framework for experimental evolution, complementing efforts to learn general representations of protein biology (56). In this framework, an informative joint embedding space allows the model to reason about mutation's impact on desired protein phenotype through understanding laboratory experiments. This provides foundation for protein engineering in which virtual exploration and experimental learning advance together toward desired function, broadly enabling the synthetic biology and molecular engineering community to select for protein sequences with the desired phenotype efficiently.

sections.title: Overview of the ProTEUS world model
sections.content: ProTEUS represented protein variants in joint space of sequence, evolutionary and structural information. Mutation actions specified substitutions applied to WT or selected parental sequences, and the model predicted the fitness of the resulting candidates. Deep mutational scanning (DMS) pretraining established the shared representation, while target-specific measurements supported supervised fine-tuning or iterative prediction updates. nomination strategy connected these predictions to successive experimental batches, with returned measurements informing the next round of candidate selection.

sections.title: Deep mutational scanning datasets for pretraining and evaluation
sections.content: We assembled the pretraining data from 217 substitution deep mutational scanning (DMS) assays in ProteinGym (29). To separate pretraining from downstream evaluation, we compared assay wild-type (WT) sequences with those of 38 reference sequences from held-out datasets reserved for downstream evaluation (fig. S1A and fig. S1B). Screening used exact-sequence, bidirectional-substring and UniProt-identifier matching, followed by MMseqs2 (71) homology searches. We excluded pretraining assays with at least 30% sequence identity and 0.5 query coverage to an evaluation protein. After removal of 35 assays, the corpus contained 182 assays representing 161 distinct WT sequences and 160 UniProt entries. The pretraining assays covered proteins of 37 3,423 amino acids (median, 224) and contained 63 496,137 measured variants per assay (median, 2,238). The corpus comprised 65 stability, 61 organismal-fitness, 32 activity, 15 expression and nine binding assays, with 80 human, 41 prokaryotic, 31 other eukaryotic and 30 viral assays. We oriented experimental scores so that larger values indicated better measured performance and normalized them within each assay. Variants with unresolved sequences or reported WT residues inconsistent with the reference sequence were removed. Variants from the 182 assays were pooled and divided into training, validation and test sets in 3:1:1 ratio. The test set therefore assessed prediction on held-out variants from pretraining assays (Fig. 2B). Each architecture comparison used the same held-out variants for all models within that comparison (Fig. 2D). Zero-shot prediction and target-specific supervised fine-tuning were evaluated on 19 assays excluded from pretraining. The zero-shot benchmark retained the available mixture of singleand multi-substitution variants in each assay first-round nomination benchmark used 13 single-substitution assays (Fig. 2F). Trainable parameters were initialized from DMS pretraining and optimized against target-assay measurements using the same MSE objective. The trainable components are specified in table S2. Fivefold cross-validation was performed independently for each assay, with four folds used for fine-tuning and the remaining fold for evaluation. Fold assignments were identical across methods, and metrics were averaged over folds within each assay. Single-mutant evolution was evaluated over five rounds on CALM1, GAL4, HRAS, MAPK1, TPK1, TPMT, UBE2I, UBI4, beta-lactamase and HaeIII methyltransferase datasets (Fig. 2H). ProTEUS and EVOLVEpro (3) each selected 30 variants per round from the same candidate library for each dataset. Accumulated measurements were used to update fitness predictions before each subsequent round of selection. At each round, we calculated the fraction of nominated variants belonging to the top 5%, 10% or 20% of the complete DMS dataset, with Precision@10 additionally compared across 14 datasets at batch sizes of 30, 50 and 100 variants per round (fig. S3AC). The best fitness recovered by that round was normalized to the observed fitness range of the dataset. Round-wise trajectories report the mean normalized best fitness across datasets. Physics-constrained all-atom structure prediction We developed an all-atom predictor to generate variant-specific structures for multi-mutant candidates (Fig. 3AE). The predictor retained the atom-attention encoder, MSA stack, PairFormer and diffusion coordinate module of Boltz-1 and was initialized from its publicly released weights (43). We fine-tuned the predictor with the denoising loss evaluated on projected coordinates, as described below (32). At inference, two denoising steps used molecular conditioning features to estimate denoised coordinates and update the noisy coordinates: (10) Here, indexes the two steps; is the denoiser and contains molecular conditioning features. denotes centered, randomly augmented coordinates after noise injection, is the denoised estimate, is the noise level after inflation, is the scheduled next noise level and is the step factor. We retained the original noise parameterization and denoising objective and used the two-step schedule at inference (32, 75). Coordinates after the second update were corrected by differentiable projection. The projection enforced seven constraint families: nonbonded inter-chain steric separation, tetrahedral chirality, double-bond E/Z stereochemistry, carbon double-bond planarity, ligand internal-distance geometry, separation of symmetric chains and covalent bonds spanning separate chains (table S3). Each was expressed as hinge residual that vanished within its feasible region. Physical validity in the reported evaluation required satisfaction of all seven specified constraint families to numerical tolerance.

sections.title: Mutant library construction and expression
sections.content: Individual amino acid substitutions were introduced into Bacillus subtilis levansucrase and Cupriavidus pinatubonensis ALDH by inverse PCR using Q5 High-Fidelity DNA Polymerase (NEB). Back-to-back primers were centered on each target codon, with 1525 bp template homology on each side and melting temperatures of 6072 C. Methylated templates were digested with DpnI, and products were circularized with NEBuilder HiFi DNA Assembly Master Mix (NEB) at 50 for 1560 min. Assemblies were transformed into NEB Stable competent cells. Two to three colonies per mutant were picked and miniprepped. Sequencing confirmed the intended substitution and absence of secondary mutations across the coding region. One verified clone per mutant was retransformed into NEB Express cells for expression. Mutants were processed in batches of approximately 30 in 96-deep-well plates, alongside three WT replicates and three empty-vector controls per plate. Starter cultures contained 1 mL LB medium with antibiotic and were grown overnight at 37 and 250 rpm. Cultures were diluted 1:30 into 1.5 mL fresh medium and grown to OD₆₀₀ 0.40.6; the OD₆₀₀ at induction was recorded for each well. Expression was induced with 0.5 mM IPTG, and cultures were shifted to 25 for 46 h. Final OD₆₀₀ was recorded before harvest by centrifugation at 3,0004,000 for 15 min at 4 C.

sections.title: Activity assays for experimental screening
sections.content: Levansucrase activity was measured in CTAB-permeabilized cells. Pellets were resuspended in McIlvaines buffer (pH 6.0), normalized to the same optical density and treated with 0.1% CTAB for 10 min at 900 rpm. Sucrose was added to final concentration of 100 mM, and reactions proceeded at 37 for 5 min. Reactions were stopped by dilution into 200 mM Tris (pH 8.3) and heat inactivation at 96 for 5 min. Released glucose was quantified with the Abcam Glucose Assay Kit (ab65333) as the activity readout. ALDH activity was measured in clarified crude lysate. Pellets were resuspended in ice-cold kit assay buffer containing fresh protease inhibitors and sonicated on ice at 2030% amplitude. Sonication comprised three cycles of 10 on and 10 off. Lysates were clarified by centrifugation at 12,00015,000 for 10 min at 4 C. Lysate volumes of 1020 µL were adjusted to 50 µL with assay buffer and combined with reaction mix from the Abcam ALDH Activity Assay Kit (ab155893). NADH production was monitored using the coupled absorbance readout at 450 nm and 37 C. Activity was quantified from the slope of the initial linear region of the kinetic curve recorded over 2030 min. Enzyme quantification and concentration-normalized ALDH activity Both enzymes carried C-terminal His tag. Both enzyme concentrations were quantified using His-tag enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) kit (GenScript, L00436), following the manufacturers protocol. Standard curves were fitted in GraphPad Prism using four-parameter logistic model, with R² > 0.9 required for acceptance. Variant concentrations were estimated from the fitted curves. Measured ALDH activity was divided by enzyme concentration to obtain concentration-normalized activity. Enzyme concentration and concentration-normalized activity were each expressed relative to the corresponding WT value.

sections.title: Pretraining data and similarity analyses
sections.content: Variant sequences in the ProteinGym (29) deep mutational scanning (DMS) corpus were reconstructed from reported substitutions and the assay-specific wild-type (WT) sequence. Sequence alignments from MMseqs2 (71) were summarized by identity, query coverage and aligned length. Structural alignments from Foldseek/TMalign (82, 83) were ranked by query-normalized TM-score, retaining the best match for each reserved entry. The structural analysis included 181 available pretraining structures and 38 reserved structures. Sequence and structural summaries are shown in Fig. S1. Model training and target-specific updates The ESM-2 (12), MSA Transformer (15) and ESM3 (21) source encoders (Table S1) remained fixed. DMS pretraining jointly optimized the multimodal representation model and neural fitness head (Table S2). Target-specific neural fine-tuning updated the same trainable components. The neural fitness head used the final layer-normalized register-token embedding. This learned token was prepended to the residue sequence with mutation-mask value of zero. During iterative evolution, the pretrained representation model provided fixed inputs to target-specific random forest. The random forest was refitted after each round using all accumulated experimental measurements.

sections.title: Geometric and stereochemical constraints
sections.content: Table S3 specifies the geometric and stereochemical bounds enforced by GaussSeidel projection (32). The predictor architecture, training procedure and projection equations are described in the section Physics-constrained all-atom structure prediction.

sections.title: Computational benchmarks
sections.content: Single-mutant evolution and experimental budgets The single-mutant benchmark used one ProTEUS run (Figure 2H). EVOLVEpro (3) used mean-pooled ESM-2 15B embeddings and 100-tree random forest, with results averaged over 10 runs. The expanded analysis added AAV, GB1, GFP and TrpB to the 10 single-mutant datasets. Dataset-level Precision@10 is shown for batches of 30, 50 and 100 variants per round (Fig. S3). Best-fitness summaries cover batch sizes of 30100 in increments of 10. Normalized best-fitness values were summarized without additional rescaling. Higher-order prediction and multi-mutant evolution Higher-order predictions were compared with the MULTI-evolve supervised predictor (1) using one-sided paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests for higher Spearman correlation with ProTEUS within each group (Figure 3F). Here, is the maximum number of substitutions in training variants. Unadjusted values were 0.0133, 0.0108 and 0.0386 for = 1, 2 and 3, respectively. Multi-mutant evolution simulations used seed 42 for ProTEUS and seeds 1, 2, 42, 2025 and 2026 for the comparators (Figure 3G). Best-fitness values were minmax normalized. Comparator results were averaged over seeds within each dataset before calculating the across-dataset mean and standard error of the mean (SEM). No further rescaling was applied across methods or rounds.

sections.title: In silico comparison of nomination strategies
sections.content: We compared five nomination strategies using fixed ProTEUS representations and random-forest predictor updated after each batch (Fig. S4; Table S4). The panel comprised 13 CombinGym (46) phenotype datasets and AAV, GB1 and TrpB. For each dataset, the cumulative mean DMS score was divided by the largest cumulative mean obtained across all evaluated strategies and rounds. Across-dataset summaries report the mean and sample standard deviation (SD). The numbers of contributing datasets were 15, 16, 13, 11 and 11 in model-guided rounds 15, respectively.

sections.title: Laboratory nomination and batch selection
sections.content: Both levansucrase and aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH) campaigns began with zero-shot variant ranking. Subsequent nominations combined zero-shot ranks, updated random-forest prediction ranks and fitness ranks derived from all available experimental measurements. Each experimental batch contained 30 variants, and round labels begin at zero. Table S5 lists the parental backgrounds, substitution counts and best variants for each batch. For levansucrase, candidate nominations drew on shortlists generated under different weighting configurations. The final batch retained two parental backgrounds, comprising 18 triple mutants derived from Q34N:G240W and 12 derived from Q34N:S359F. For ALDH, five weighting configurations were evaluated for zero-shot ranks and fitness ranks derived from experimental measurements. The respective weight pairs were (0, 0.2), (0, 0.4), (0, 0.6), (0.2, 0.2) and (0.2, 0.4). The random-forest weight was one minus the sum of these two weights. Each configuration produced shortlist of 30 variants. Candidates were prioritized by the number of shortlists in which they appeared, with ties ordered by their best rank across the shortlists. The top 30 candidates were selected for experimental testing.

sections.title: Analysis of laboratory evolution campaigns
sections.content: Scoreactivity associations Scoreactivity analyses used the zero-shot ranking in round 0. In subsequent rounds, composite scores combined normalized zero-shot ranks, random-forest prediction ranks and fitness ranks derived from all available experimental measurements, with respective weights of 0.2, 0.6 and 0.2. Scores were rescaled to 01 within each round, and Spearman correlations included all 30 assayed variants. For levansucrase, composite scores were analyzed in rounds 1 and 2. For ALDH, the reference sequence was UniProt P46368. All nine nonpositive activity measurements were retained in the scoreactivity analysis. Cumulative best-activity and top-ten summaries included all variants tested up to each round.

sections.title: Protein representations and geometric analyses
sections.content: For levansucrase, sucrose from PDB 1PT2 was transferred to WT SacB (PDB 1OYG) after Cα-based structural superposition. Residuesubstrate distances were the minimum heavy-atom separations between each WT residue and the superposed sucrose. For ALDH, substitutions were mapped to WT model AF-P46368-F1. Distances to the catalytic site were the minimum heavy-atom separations between each WT residue and either Glu262 or Cys301. Quantitative representation analyses used the original 768-dimensional vectors. Candidate libraries and assayed variants were visualized using t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE). Parentchild relationships were defined by shared and newly introduced substitutions. For levansucrase, mean-pooled ProTEUS representations were available for WT and 90 assayed variants. The candidate background contained 366,836 library entries across single-, doubleand triple-mutant libraries. The t-SNE map was fitted to 20,000 points balanced across these libraries, and the remaining entries were projected into the fitted map. Within each final-round parental background, we compared cosine distances among pairs at amino acid Hamming distance two. Principal component analysis (PCA) of mean-centered representations determined the number of components explaining 90% of the variance; the comparator encoded the final amino acid at each variable position by one-hot encoding (Table S9). For measured levansucrase parentchild pairs, the mutational displacement was the child representation minus the parental representation. We compared the two displacement vectors for I369H, the only added substitution tested on both final-round parents. For ALDH, all variants were encoded with the same pretrained 12-layer checkpoint. Final encoder states were averaged over valid positions, including the register token and excluding padding. The candidate background contained 9,615 single-substitution, 153,402 double-substitution, 47,873 triple-substitution and 143,254 four-substitution library entries, totaling 354,144. Counts describe library entries rather than deduplicated sequences. The 150 assayed variants and WT were matched to their representations by substitution identity. The ALDH projection used subset stratified across the four candidate libraries, reduced to 50 dimensions by PCA. We fitted t-SNE with openTSNE (51, 84), using perplexity 50, PCA initialization and random seed 42. Remaining library entries, assayed variants and WT were transformed using the same PCA basis and fitted t-SNE map.

sections.title: Local activity association
sections.content: We compared absolute activity differences between embedding neighbors with those between sequence-distance-matched variants. Neighbors were defined by cosine distance in the original representation space, excluding the anchor itself. For each directed anchorneighbor pair, the reference set contained all variants in the same analysis group at the same amino acid Hamming distance from the anchor, including the selected neighbor. Hamming distance counted residue positions that differed between variants. Differences were averaged within anchors before aggregation across variants. The statistic was the matched-reference mean absolute activity difference (MAD) minus the neighbor MAD; relative reduction was one minus the ratio of neighbor MAD to reference MAD. Activity labels were permuted 19,999 times within analysis groups, keeping neighborhoods and sequence-distance matrices fixed. Two-sided values were twice the smaller tail probability, with plus-one correction and maximum of 1. Variants were the permutation units, and all recorded activities were retained. For levansucrase, the analysis included the 30 triple mutants from the final round, comprising 18 descendants of Q34N:G240W and 12 of Q34N:S359F. Neighbors, reference sets and label permutations were restricted to each parental background. All 30 anchors were weighted equally. We evaluated three, five and ten neighbors, using random seed 20261028. For ALDH, the analysis included the 60 four-substitution variants from rounds 3 and 4. Neighbors, reference sets and label permutations were restricted to each experimental batch. Differences were averaged across variants within each batch and then equally across the two batches. Five neighbors defined the primary analysis; three and ten neighbors were used for sensitivity analyses (Table S6). The random seed was 20261019.

Evaluation used round 0 to predict round 1, rounds 01 to predict round 2, and nested leave-one-out prediction within round 2. Model selection used training data only. For ALDH, the 30 round-3 variants formed the training set and the 30 round-4 variants formed the test set. All variants shared the same parental background and substitution count. Intervals describe test-variant uncertainty conditional on the observed training data and activity measurements. Alignment-based substitution frequencies At each substituted position, we counted occurrences of the introduced amino acid among homologous sequences. The originality ratio was the introduced-residue count divided by the highest amino acid count at the same position. ratio of 1 denoted consensus residue, and 0 denoted residue not observed at that position in the alignment. Campaign-level summaries counted each distinct substitution once. For levansucrase, the alignment contained 2,451 homologous sequences. Frequencies used the number of sequences aligned without gap at the respective position as the denominator. Summary frequencies covered 89 distinct substitutions. sections.title: Similarity to the pretraining set
sections.content: Structural comparisons identified related folds among held-out targets with low sequence identity to the pretraining set. Of the 38 held-out reference sequences, 20 had closest structural match with query-normalized TM-score of at least 0.5. Sequence identities for these matches ranged from 1% to 25% (Fig. S1B). Zero-shot fitness prediction Across the 19 held-out assays, ProTEUS ranked third by NDCG and second by top-10% recall (Fig. S2A). In the 13 single-mutant assays, ProTEUS had the highest mean Spearman correlation, whereas its NDCG and top-10% recall were slightly lower than those of the four-score MULTI-evolve rank-fusion comparator (Fig. S2B).

sections.title: Simulated evolution across datasets and experimental budgets
sections.content: ProTEUS achieved higher Precision@10 than EVOLVEpro in 10, 9 and 10 of the 14 datasets at batch sizes of 30, 50 and 100 variants per round, respectively (Fig. S3). With 30 variants selected per round, ProTEUS exceeded the mean EVOLVEpro result in 10 of 14 datasets by round 5. ProTEUS reached its final best fitness in round 1 for UBE2I, whereas GB1 and TrpB improved subsequently. EVOLVEpro recovered higher final best fitness for CALM1, GAL4, HRAS and GFP.

sections.title: In silico comparison of nomination strategies
sections.content: The five nomination strategies differed in their use of zero-shot ranking, updated fitness predictions and fitness ranks derived from all available experimental measurements (Fig. S4; Table S4). Strategy achieved the highest across-dataset mean normalized cumulative DMS score in each evaluated round. By round 5, the mean was 0.886, compared with 0.866 for the updated predictor alone and 0.804 for the two-component ranking. The contributing datasets differed among rounds, with counts specified in the Fig. S4 legend.

sections.title: Exploratory analysis of laboratory activities
sections.content: Among final-round levansucrase variants, the five-neighbor mean absolute activity difference was 3.524, compared with 3.030 for Hamming-distance-matched references (two-sided permutation = 0.176). Prediction of round 2 from rounds 01 gave MAEs of 2.007 for embedding ridge regression and 2.992 for embedding random forest, compared with 2.007 for the training mean. Thus, these activity-based analyses did not show an advantage for the embedding readouts in the final round. Prediction from the preceding ALDH batch yielded Spearman correlation of 0.26 (95% confidence interval, 0.10 to 0.59; two-sided permutation = 0.158). MAE was 1.60 for the embedding-neighbor predictor, compared with 1.71 for the training-mean comparator and 1.80 for the training-median comparator (Table S7). The estimated MAE reduction relative to the training mean was 0.12 (95% confidence interval, 0.16 to 0.39). Hamming-distance ties gave every training variant equal weight, producing the same predictions as the training-mean comparator. The intervals included zero correlation and zero MAE reduction, leaving prediction across these batches unresolved for this nearest-neighbor readout.
